title: collections.Counter
summary: A dict subclass for counting hashable things, with `most_common` and arithmetic between counters.
description: Counting is common enough to deserve a type. A missing key reads as 0 rather than raising, which removes the initialisation branch from every counting loop.

parameters.name: iterable_or_mapping
parameters.description: Items to count, or initial counts.

examples.title: Counting words
examples.code:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter('the the cat'.split()))

examples.title: Missing keys are zero, and are not inserted
examples.code:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter(a=1)
print(c['zzz'], 'zzz' in c)

examples.title: Arithmetic
examples.code:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter(a=3, b=1) - Counter(a=1))

real_world_usage: Word and event frequencies, finding the noisiest alert rule, detecting duplicates, and comparing two inventories with subtraction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Relying on most_common to break ties
common_mistakes.fix: Ties come out in insertion order, which is not alphabetical. Sort explicitly with a key when the tie-break matters.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting a KeyError for a missing key
common_mistakes.fix: It returns 0. Use `in` when you need to know whether it was ever seen.

performance_notes: Counting is O(n) with dict-level constants. most_common(k) uses a heap and is O(n log k); most_common() with no argument sorts everything, O(n log n).
security_notes: Counting untrusted distinct values is unbounded memory. Cap the number of distinct keys you will track.
